name: Payment Services Directive 2 (PSD2)
evidence_rating: moderate: Commission evaluation with market data; cross-country causal evidence on open banking; little independent evidence on prices or SCA trade-offs
summary: PSD2's strong customer authentication cut card fraud sharply (70-80% lower on authenticated remote payments) and open-banking rules helped new payment firms enter; cross-country research links open banking to more fintech investment. But open-banking uptake is uneven, banks report high API costs, card markets stay national and the promised fall in payment costs for merchants has not materialised. Industry data point to some lost online sales from authentication friction.

indicators.objective: Develop an EU-wide market for electronic payments
Address standardisation and interoperability gaps for card, internet and mobile payments
Eliminate hurdles for competition, in particular for card and internet payments
Align charging and steering practices across the EU
Cover emerging payment services and instruments
Ensure consistent application of licensing and supervision across Member States
Ensure adequate and consistent consumer protection

indicators.indicator: Commission assessment of implementation and impact, based on a conformity check and a market study (no quantified indicators set)
indicators.evidence: Done: Commission review COM(2023) 365 and evaluation (with SWD(2023) 231). Finds 'varying degrees of success'.
Clear success: SCA-authenticated remote card payments show 70-80% lower fraud than non-SCA ones.

indicators.indicator: Facilitate innovative payment services (open banking, new entrants)
indicators.evidence: Mixed: hundreds of new non-bank providers with millions of clients, but open-banking uptake uneven and data-access interfaces of variable quality; banks report high API costs. Cross-country evidence: open-banking policies spur fintech investment (Babina et al.).

indicators.indicator: Downward convergence of costs and prices for payment users
indicators.evidence: Not achieved yet: anticipated cost reductions for merchants from cheaper payment methods 'have not yet fully materialised'; card systems remain largely national; no pan-European solution yet.
Surcharging ban covers 95% of EU payments; Commission sees no need for further alignment.

literature.citation: European Commission (2013), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for PSD2 and the Interchange Fee Regulation (summary SWD(2013) 289), SWD(2013) 288
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for PSD2 and the Interchange Fee Regulation (summary SWD(2013) 289)
literature.headline: Package-level estimates: card standardisation benefits ~EUR 4bn/yr; interchange-fee caps EUR 3-6bn/yr operational savings for merchants (these relate mainly to the Interchange Fee Regulation, not PSD2)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the payments package to save merchants and consumers billions a year, mostly through caps on card fees set in a separate regulation.
literature.quality: forecast; most quantified benefits belong to the companion Interchange Fee Regulation

literature.citation: European Commission (2023), Report on the review of Directive (EU) 2015/2366 (PSD2), COM(2023) 365, with evaluation in SWD(2023) 231
literature.title: Report on the review of Directive (EU) 2015/2366 (PSD2)
literature.headline: SCA highly successful against fraud (70-80% lower fraud on SCA remote card payments); new non-bank entrants and open-banking growth but uneven uptake and poor API performance; merchant cost reductions not yet materialised; card systems still national
literature.summary_plain: PSD2 sharply reduced card fraud and let many new payment firms enter, but open banking has taken off unevenly and promised savings for merchants have not yet appeared.

literature.citation: Babina, Bahaj, Buchak, De Marco, Foulis, Gornall, Mazzola & Yu (2024), Customer Data Access and Fintech Entry: Early Evidence from Open Banking, NBER Working Paper 32089 (also Bank of England staff working paper)
literature.authors: Babina, Bahaj, Buchak, De Marco, Foulis, Gornall, Mazzola & Yu
literature.title: Customer Data Access and Fintech Entry: Early Evidence from Open Banking
literature.venue: NBER Working Paper 32089 (also Bank of England staff working paper)
literature.method: causal: cross-country staggered adoption (49 countries) + UK microdata + calibrated model
literature.headline: Open-banking adoption spurs investment in fintechs; in the UK it gives consumers access to advice and credit and SMEs new fintech lending relationships; welfare gains from advice, mixed for credit (higher prices for costlier or privacy-conscious consumers)
literature.summary_plain: Across 49 countries, open-banking rules like those in PSD2 attracted more investment into fintech start-ups and widened access to credit, though some consumers end up paying more.
literature.quality: not EU-specific; PSD2 is one of the policies studied

literature.citation: MultiSafepay (2021), How PSD2 & Strong Customer Authentication affect your payment success rates, Industry blog (payment service provider)
literature.title: How PSD2 & Strong Customer Authentication affect your payment success rates
literature.headline: Average conversion for 3DS-authenticated card payments about 82%; gap vs non-authenticated flows about 7% in NL and about 13% in IT and ES
literature.summary_plain: Payment-industry data suggest the extra authentication step costs online shops some sales, with bigger losses in southern Europe.
literature.quality: vendor data; not independent; no counterfactual
